Households and firms exchange factor services, incomes, goods and consumption expenditure. Add government, financial institutions and foreign trade to show leakages and injections.

AD-AS
Aggregate demand is total planned expenditure at different price levels. Aggregate supply represents production conditions. A rightward AD shift can raise output and price level when spare capacity exists. Near capacity, the price effect may dominate.

KEYNESIAN CROSS
Plot planned aggregate expenditure against real output. The 45-degree line shows where expenditure equals output. An increase in autonomous expenditure shifts planned expenditure upward and increases equilibrium income.

MULTIPLIER
The size of the multiplier depends on marginal propensities to consume, save, tax and import. More leakages mean a smaller multiplier.

INFLATIONARY GAP
An economy producing above a sustainable capacity level may experience demand pressure and inflation. Policy can aim to reduce excess demand or expand productive capacity.

RECESSIONARY GAP
Output below potential can be associated with cyclical unemployment and unused capacity. Expansionary demand management may increase output if inflation constraints are limited.

PHILLIPS CURVE
A short-run curve may illustrate a possible inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment. Expectations can shift the relationship, so the curve should not be treated as a permanent policy menu.

MONEY MARKET
Interest rate can be represented as the price of liquidity. A rightward shift in money demand can raise interest rates in a standard framework if supply is fixed.

LABOUR MARKET
A minimum wage above equilibrium creates excess labour supply in the basic competitive model. Discuss empirical conditions before generalising.

FOREIGN EXCHANGE
Demand for a currency can arise from exports and capital flows; supply can arise from imports and outward flows. Exchange-rate changes affect competitiveness and domestic prices.

BALANCE OF PAYMENTS
A current-account deficit may correspond with net financial inflows under accounting identities. The economic issue is whether financing is sustainable and whether the deficit reflects productive investment or persistent structural weakness.

LORenz CURVE
The Lorenz curve plots cumulative population against cumulative income. Greater distance from the line of equality indicates greater inequality.

DEVELOPMENT INDICATORS
No single diagram captures development. Combine income indicators with health, education, employment, infrastructure and environmental indicators.

DIAGRAM EVALUATION
State assumptions. For example, an AD increase may have different price/output effects depending on spare capacity, supply elasticity and expectations.

subject: Economics
content:
GDP VS GNI
GDP concerns production within a country's territory. GNI focuses on income accruing to residents/nationals under the relevant statistical definition. The two can differ when cross-border factor income is substantial.

NOMINAL VS REAL
Nominal uses current prices. Real attempts to remove price effects.

GDP VS GDP PER CAPITA
GDP is total output. GDP per capita divides by population and is therefore a rougher indicator of average material output/income.

GROWTH VS DEVELOPMENT
Growth is quantitative expansion of real output. Development includes broader improvements in welfare and capabilities.

INFLATION VS PRICE INCREASE
Inflation is a sustained increase in the general price level. A one-off increase in one product price is not, by itself, inflation.

DEFLATION VS DISINFLATION
Deflation means the general price level falls. Disinflation means inflation continues but at a lower rate.

DEVALUATION VS DEPRECIATION
Devaluation is an official downward adjustment under a fixed/managed arrangement. Depreciation is a fall in value under market-based exchange-rate movement.

UNEMPLOYMENT VS INACTIVITY
Unemployed people are generally without work and actively seeking/available for work under the statistical definition. Economically inactive people are not counted as unemployed because they are not seeking/available in the relevant sense.

PRIVATE GOOD VS PUBLIC GOOD
Private goods can be excludable and rival. Pure public goods are non-excludable and non-rival.

EXTERNAL COST VS PRIVATE COST
Private cost is borne by the decision-maker. External cost is imposed on third parties.

ACCOUNTING PROFIT VS ECONOMIC PROFIT
Accounting profit subtracts explicit monetary costs. Economic profit also accounts for opportunity costs.

NORMAL VS SUPERNORMAL PROFIT
Normal profit is the minimum return needed to keep enterprise in the activity. Supernormal profit is profit above that amount.

ECONOMIC RENT VS TRANSFER EARNINGS
Economic rent is reward above transfer earnings. Transfer earnings are the minimum needed to keep a factor in current use.

STOCK VS FLOW
A stock is measured at a point in time, such as wealth or debt. A flow is measured over a period, such as income or investment.

WEALTH VS INCOME
Wealth is a stock of assets minus liabilities. Income is a flow over a period.

SAVING VS INVESTMENT
Saving is income not consumed. Investment is expenditure on capital goods or productive assets in macroeconomic accounting.

CURRENT ACCOUNT VS CAPITAL/FINANCIAL FLOWS
The current account records trade and relevant income/transfers; financial flows record investment and other financing transactions under the applicable statistical framework.

PRICE ELASTICITY VS INCOME ELASTICITY
PED measures response to own price. YED measures response to income.

SUBSTITUTE VS COMPLEMENT
Substitutes compete for similar uses; complements are consumed together or in connected use.

FIXED COST VS SUNK COST
A fixed cost does not vary with output over a relevant short run. A sunk cost cannot be recovered. A cost can be fixed without being sunk and vice versa.

subject: Economics
topic: Full-Length Revision Questions with Answer Frameworks
content:
QUESTION 1: Explain why opportunity cost is unavoidable.
Framework: scarcity → choice → alternative uses → next-best alternative → example.

QUESTION 2: Analyse factors determining PED.
Framework: substitutes → necessity/luxury → income share → time → brand loyalty → conclusion.

QUESTION 3: Explain how an indirect tax affects market equilibrium.
Framework: tax raises marginal cost → supply shifts → consumer price rises → producer receipt falls → quantity falls → incidence depends on elasticities.

QUESTION 4: Discuss whether subsidies always benefit consumers.
Framework: lower cost → supply shift → lower price/higher quantity → fiscal cost → targeting/leakage → long-run incentive effects.

QUESTION 5: Evaluate monopoly.
Framework: market power → price/output → consumer surplus → possible economies of scale → innovation → regulation → judgement.

QUESTION 6: Explain why wages differ.
Framework: labour demand → productivity/MRP → labour supply → skills → compensating differentials → institutions → discrimination.

QUESTION 7: Discuss whether free trade is always beneficial.
Framework: comparative advantage → consumer benefits → competition → adjustment costs → infant industry → retaliation → judgement.

QUESTION 8: Explain causes of inflation.
Framework: demand-pull → cost-push → expectations → imported inflation → money/credit conditions where relevant → distinguish causes by evidence.

QUESTION 9: Evaluate fiscal policy during recession.
Framework: higher G/lower taxes → AD → multiplier → employment → debt/crowding-out → time lags → supply capacity → conclusion.

QUESTION 10: Evaluate monetary policy to reduce inflation.
Framework: interest rates → borrowing/consumption/investment → AD → inflation → exchange rate → debt burden → supply-shock limitation.

QUESTION 11: Explain balance-of-payments disequilibrium.
Framework: trade balance → income/transfers → capital/financial flows → structural causes → financing → sustainability.

QUESTION 12: Discuss depreciation as a solution to a trade deficit.
Framework: import price effect → export competitiveness → elasticities → J-curve → imported inflation → capacity constraints → conclusion.

QUESTION 13: Explain the benefits of economic development.
Framework: health → education → employment → productivity → infrastructure → poverty/inequality → sustainability.

QUESTION 14: Evaluate foreign direct investment.
Framework: capital → jobs → technology → tax/export effects → profit repatriation → crowding out → environmental/regulatory concerns → judgement.

QUESTION 15: Discuss whether government should redistribute income.
Framework: equity rationale → progressive tax/transfers → incentives → administration → human capital → poverty reduction → efficiency trade-off → conclusion.

subject: Economics
content:
INFLATION POLICY
When evaluating anti-inflation policy in Zimbabwe, identify whether the pressure is demand-side, supply-side, exchange-rate-related, imported, expectation-driven or a combination. Avoid assuming that interest-rate policy alone can fix shortages or imported-cost shocks.

EXCHANGE RATE
Analyse the exchange rate through imports, exports, inflation, foreign-currency availability, expectations and productive capacity. A depreciation can help exporters only if firms can expand supply and foreign demand responds.

AGRICULTURE
Agricultural productivity can influence food prices, rural incomes, employment, imports and exports. Consider climate risk, irrigation, input availability, finance, extension, storage and transport.

MINING
Mining can generate exports and foreign exchange but creates exposure to commodity-price cycles. Value addition and diversification can retain more economic value domestically.

MANUFACTURING
Manufacturing benefits from reliable energy, transport, skills, finance and predictable input markets. Imported input dependence creates exchange-rate vulnerability.

INFORMAL ECONOMY
The informal sector can absorb labour and generate livelihoods but may face limited finance, weak social protection and low productivity. Policies should consider both formalisation and livelihood protection.

SMEs
SMEs can support entrepreneurship and employment. Constraints may include finance, markets, infrastructure, skills, regulation and technology.

PUBLIC DEBT
Borrowing for productive infrastructure may support long-run capacity, while borrowing for recurrent consumption may create different sustainability issues. Always examine the purpose and return on borrowing.

TAXATION
A tax can raise revenue and alter behaviour. Evaluation should consider the tax base, compliance, incidence, administrative cost and effects on incentives.

SUBSIDIES
Targeted subsidies may protect vulnerable households or strategic production, but broad subsidies can be expensive and distort incentives.

TRADE POLICY
Protection may support an infant industry temporarily but can reduce competitive pressure. A successful policy should specify why the industry needs protection, what performance target applies and when support should end.

DEVELOPMENT
Development strategies should link economic growth to employment, human capital, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, equality and environmental sustainability.

POLICY CREDIBILITY
Stable and predictable policy can affect investment decisions. Frequent policy changes may increase uncertainty and risk premiums.

DATA CAUTION
When using Zimbabwe examples, distinguish official statistics, survey evidence, estimates and anecdotal claims. State the source and period when data are supplied in an exam question.
